text: You have n tasks, labeled zero to n minus one. Each task is an enqueue time and a processing time: task i becomes available at its enqueue time and takes its processing time to finish. A single-threaded CPU runs one task at a time. If it's idle and nothing is available, it stays idle. If it's idle and tasks are available, it picks the one with the shortest processing time, and on a tie, the smallest index. Once it starts a task, it runs it to the end, and it can start the next one right away. Return the order the CPU processes the tasks.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the CPU only makes a choice when it becomes free. So a short task that arrives in the middle of a long task has to wait. It can't cut in. Right?
And a task that arrives at the exact moment the CPU becomes free counts as available? So available means enqueue time less than or equal to the current time?
Yes, it can be picked at that moment.
Are there any constraints on the input size?
n is between one and ten to the fifth. Both times are between one and ten to the ninth.

OK, two things jump out. First, n is up to ten to the fifth, so I need about n log n. Second, the total time can reach ten to the fifth times ten to the ninth, which is ten to the fourteenth. That doesn't fit in an int, so my clock has to be a long long. Let me run through the example: one-two, two-four, three-two, four-one. Task zero runs alone from one to three. The real decision is at three: tasks one and two are both waiting, and the shorter task two wins. Task three arrives meanwhile and is the shortest, then task one. So the answer is zero, two, three, one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to simulate, and each time the CPU is free, scan all the tasks that have arrived and aren't done, and pick the best one. That's correct, but it's linear per pick, so quadratic in total. With ten to the fifth tasks, that's around ten to the tenth. Too slow. This problem reminds me of an event-driven simulation with a heap. Two parts. Tasks arrive in enqueue-time order, so I sort the indices by enqueue time and walk them with one pointer. Among the tasks that have arrived, I need the best one quickly — that's a min-heap keyed by processing time, then index. Each task goes into the heap once and comes out once, so this is n log n.

Here's the plan. One: sort the indices by enqueue time. Two: if the heap is empty, jump the clock to the next arrival, then push every task that has arrived. Three: pop the best task, run it, and add its time to the clock. One thing worth flagging — the heap key needs both parts. Processing time first: shorter wins. Index second: a heap is not stable, so I can't rely on push order to break ties; it has to be in the comparator. And the idle jump must be a max. The clock must never go backwards. There's a trade-off here. I could tick the clock one step at a time. Same answer, but a gap of ten to the ninth would mean ten to the ninth loop steps. The jump takes one. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The heap stores indices, not copies of the tasks, and the comparator looks the task up through the reference capture. In a priority queue, a greater-than comparator puts the smallest on top. So greater-than on processing time, then a greater than b on the index, gives shortest first, then smallest index. One thing worth flagging — the inner while uses t greater than or equal to the enqueue time, not strictly greater. Right after the idle jump, t equals the next enqueue time exactly. With a strict greater-than, nothing gets pushed, and the top call runs on an empty heap. That breaks on every input.

Let's dry-run the code with an example. Example one: arr is already zero, one, two, three, and I expect zero, two, three, one. The highlighted row is the key one. Task zero ends at three. By then tasks one and two have both arrived, so they compete, and the shorter task two wins. Then task three arrives while task two runs, and it beats task one too. That matches. Example two: all five arrive at seven, so they pop by length, giving four, three, two, zero, one. Corner cases: a single task returns just zero. On ties, one-one, two-one, one-one returns zero, one, two, because index breaks the tie. A huge idle gap jumps the clock in one step. And without the max, example one sends the clock back from three to two, task two never competes, and I'd get zero, one, two, three.

Let me think about complexity here. The time complexity is n log n. The sort is n log n, and each task is pushed once and popped once, at log n each. The outer loop runs exactly n times, because every pass pops one task, so empty time costs nothing. The space complexity is linear, for arr, the heap, and the answer. In the worst-case scenario all tasks arrive at time one, so the heap holds all ten to the fifth at once — that runs in about forty-three milliseconds, and a random input in about sixty. One note on the clock: an int would overflow, and the sanitizer flags it, yet the output never changes. To overflow, t must pass about one point one four seven billion, and by then every task is already in the heap. It's still undefined behavior, so it's a long long.
Why not just tick the clock forward by one while the CPU is idle? It's simpler.

It's correct, but the cost depends on the values, not on n. For two tasks, one at time one and one at time ten to the ninth, ticking takes over a billion loop steps, about five hundred fifty milliseconds. The jump takes two steps. Since times reach ten to the ninth, ticking is a real time-limit risk. Oh, one more thing — the max in the jump is what makes the jump safe. The jump only moves the clock forward when the CPU is idle. If the CPU just finished late, the clock stays where it is. Without that one max, over six thousand of the sixty-six thousand small test inputs come out wrong.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You showed the max in the idle jump is a correctness fix, with the example one trace where the clock goes back from three to two and task two never competes. You put the index tie-break in the comparator, because a heap isn't stable. And you explained why the int clock never changed the output, but is still undefined behavior, so you used long long. Good work.
